read: full: main text pp. 1-16 (abstract, Secs. 1-6) read in full; Appendix B (data annotation, pp. 25-26) and Appendix C (p. 26) read; other appendices (examples, OOD details, prompts, pp. 17-29) skimmed
venue_now: arXiv 2211.14275 (v1, 25 Nov 2022; page 1 footer; DeepMind). The text shows no venue. The search note mentions a NeurIPS 2022 MATH-AI workshop version that it did not open, so cite the arXiv version.
what_it_is: A training-method study, not a benchmark. On GSM8K it compares outcome-based supervision (final-answer correctness only) with process-based supervision: human reasoning traces as SFT targets, and human step-correctness labels for a process-supervised reward model. The comparison spans few-shot prompting, SFT, expert-iteration RL and reward-model reranking, all on one 70B base LM (pp. 2-6). It reports two metrics: final-answer error, and trace error, the share of final-answer-correct solutions with at least one incorrect step as judged by human annotators (p. 3). Outcome supervision reaches similar final-answer error with far less supervision. Low trace error, however, needs process feedback or a reward model that emulates it (p. 2, pp. 7-8). The best system lowers trace error from the prior 14.0% to 3.4%, and final-answer error from 16.8% to 12.7% (p. 1; Table 1, p. 7).
domain: grade-school math word problems (GSM8K); MATH pre-algebra as an out-of-distribution check (p. 11)
size: GSM8K with the authors' split: 7,118 train, 256 validation, 1,319 test (p. 3). PRM training labels: 1,560 model samples on 530 problems, 9,856 step labels (p. 6). Trace-error evaluation: 200 correct-final-answer problems per model for 10 models, double-labelled (p. 6). All models are variants of the authors' 70B base LM (Table 1, p. 7).
source_of_items: existing dataset (GSM8K); model-generated solutions labelled by trained human annotators
has_gold_traces: partial: GSM8K's human-written reference solutions serve as SFT targets and are shown to annotators (pp. 3-6); there are no machine-checkable intermediate values, and the authors 'lack reliable programmatic means for determining the correctness of intermediate steps' (p. 4)
evaluation: final answer (exact match on integer answers, p. 3) plus human step annotation of the first major mistake, reported as trace error (pp. 3, 6); no automatic step evaluator is validated
human_validation: Annotators passed a qualification test (21 of 91 candidates, p. 25). Training labels: 20% of problems double-labelled; annotators below 75% agreement removed, which dropped about 20% of the data (pp. 6, 25-26). After filtering, agreement on the first incorrect step was 92%, Cohen's kappa .915, which the authors note is biased upward (p. 26). Evaluation labels: 87% agreement but Cohen's kappa only .34 on whether the full trace is correct, which the authors attribute to subtle errors in correct-answer solutions (p. 26). Trace errors carry min-max ranges across raters, e.g. 3.4 (0.0-6.8) (Table 1, p. 7).

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it. It belongs in the new paragraph on process supervision and judge validity. Its trace-error metric is the quantity behind EngTrace's hard case: 93 of 228 correct-answer X1 traces contain an incorrect step (state brief Sec. 3). The batch description says trace error among answer-correct solutions was 'cut from 14.0% to 3.4% only with process supervision'. That is imprecise on both numbers. The 14.0% is the prior state of the art (few-shot PaLM-540B; Table 1, p. 7), not an outcome-supervised baseline. The 3.4% system is SFT plus RL against an outcome-supervised reward model (Table 1, p. 7), which the paper argues emulates process feedback (p. 8). The supportable contrast: RL directly against final-answer correctness reached a trace error of 12.4% at best, against 3.8% for the best process-based method (p. 2).

suggested_wording: Uesato et al. (2022) first compared outcome- and process-based supervision on GSM8K and showed that final-answer correctness hides flawed reasoning. Models trained by reinforcement learning against final-answer correctness alone left at best 12.4% of their correct answers resting on a human-flagged incorrect step, against 3.8% with process-based supervision.
facts_to_cite: First comprehensive comparison of process- and outcome-based supervision on a natural-language task, GSM8K, with a 70B base LM (abstract, p. 1; p. 2).
Trace error: the fraction of correct-final-answer solutions with at least one incorrect reasoning step, estimated from human step annotations (p. 3).
Outcome- and process-based training give similar final-answer error: 23.5% vs 22.3% without reward models, 16.6% vs 14.8% with them (p. 2).
RL directly against final-answer correctness gave a best trace error of 12.4%, against 3.8% for the best process-based method; RL against a reward model brought it to 5.5% (p. 2).
Best system: trace error 14.0% -> 3.4% and final-answer error 16.8% -> 12.7%; the 14.0% is the prior state of the art, few-shot PaLM-540B (abstract, p. 1; Table 1, p. 7).
Reward models trained only on outcome labels agree more with step-level process labels than with outcome labels: 85% vs 77% over all steps (p. 8).

Process labels needed humans because the authors 'lack reliable programmatic means for determining the correctness of intermediate steps' (p. 4). A heuristic that string-matches intermediate results (Li et al., 2022) did slightly worse: 15.9% final-answer error (p. 9).
Annotators agreed on whether a full trace is correct 87% of the time, but Cohen's kappa was only .34, lower than on training labels, because errors behind correct final answers are subtle (p. 26).
The authors expect process and outcome feedback to align more closely in math than in other domains, since incorrect traces rarely reach correct answers there (pp. 8, 13).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the process-versus-outcome question at the step level, and the trace-error measurement that EngTrace's hard case repeats on engineering traces. In EngTrace, 93 of 228 correct-answer X1 traces have an incorrect step: 178 steps, of which 175 are calculation slips and 3 conceptual (state brief Sec. 3). Uesato's step labels come from trained annotators; EngTrace's come from three own-branch experts per trace (Fleiss kappa 0.781 on steps). Uesato reports Cohen's kappa .34 on whole-trace correctness, a different statistic on a different task, so the two are not directly comparable. Lacks: engineering; generated instances (GSM8K is static); machine-checkable gold intermediate values, the 'programmatic means' Uesato lacked, which EngTrace's template code supplies; any automatic evaluator validated against the human labels. EngTrace's planted-defect test also sets a limit on those checks: they catch arithmetic slips but none of 60 conceptual defects. Uesato is a training study, not a benchmark.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity. It can also support the introduction's claim that a correct answer does not certify the trace. The paper is internally inconsistent. Its conclusion (p. 15) attributes the 3.4% trace error to 'SFT with PRM reranking' and gives the outcome-based analogue 12.7% trace error. Table 1 (p. 7) gives SFT with PRM reranking 3.5% and SFT+ORM-RL 3.4%. The 12.7% is SFT+ORM-RL's final-answer error; the outcome analogue's trace error is 12.4%. Cite Table 1 and the key-results paragraph (p. 2), not the conclusion. Lightman et al. (2023), already cited in the May text, builds directly on this paper; cite the two together.
